The disputed fact is Patrick Flynn's birthplace. The 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill County censuses record Ireland; his 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate records Pennsylvania. Birthplace matters because it determines whether Patrick immigrated as a child with his parents or was Pennsylvania-born — directly relevant to identifying his parentage and Irish origins.

The 1850 census (a_002) lists Patrick, age 5, birthplace Ireland, reported by an unidentified household informant — almost certainly a parent or close household member — to the enumerator. The Ancestry transcription (a_007) reproduces the same datum from the same original document and adds no independent weight. The 1860 census (a_009) lists Patrick, age 15, again with birthplace Ireland, from another unidentified household informant. The 1908 death certificate (a_012) records birthplace as Pennsylvania, supplied by James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, in 1908 — more than 60 years after Patrick's birth, by a man who did not witness it.

The two census records are more reliable. Their informants — Patrick's parents or other adult household members present during his childhood — were among the most proximately positioned informants possible for a child's birthplace, and they reported the fact contemporaneously. Two records from different census years returning the same answer strengthen the Ireland reading considerably. The death certificate informant had no first-hand knowledge of events from 1845, and death certificates completed by distant informants are well-established as unreliable for the deceased's birthplace.

James Brown's Pennsylvania answer reflects a documented informant-error pattern: long-term residence substituted for foreign birthplace. Patrick lived in Pennsylvania from at least 1850 through his 1908 death — 58 or more years. A son-in-law who never knew Patrick in Ireland and saw Pennsylvania as his lifelong home had no family knowledge pointing to Ireland. When asked for a birthplace on the death certificate, such an informant typically reports the state associated with the deceased's entire known life rather than a foreign origin he never witnessed and may never have been told about. This is the classic 'American home as birthplace' failure mode on immigrant vital records: the informant reports the family's long-established residence as the place of birth.

In practice, most researchers treat a high-quality image of an unaltered government original as functionally equivalent to the original because it represents the record as created. The Genealogical Proof Standard literature calls such a scan a **derivative created without alteration**, which carries near-original weight. fields.weighing_analysis: Three factors are decisive. (1) Patronymic encoding: Norway used active patronymics through the 19th century — the fixed-surname law came only in 1923. 'Pedersen' encodes son of Peder; 'Hansen' encodes son of Hans. These are phonetically and structurally distinct given names, not spelling variants of each other. An enumerator substituting an entirely different father's name (Peder for Hans) is a qualitatively different error from an age rounding or orthographic slip, and requires a specific explanation, not merely an acknowledgment of possibility. The household member reporting to the enumerator would normally know the father's given name with certainty; this fact was not abstract genealogical knowledge but the identity of the person living in or associated with the household. (2) Convergence of given name, age, and place: the exact match on given name (Anders), approximate birth year (~1868), and district (Ringsaker, Hedmark) is strong circumstantial evidence pointing toward identity. In a small rural district, two boys named Anders born in the same year are possible but would be unusual, particularly if traditional naming after grandfathers produced the given name in both families. (3) No defensible GPS rationale currently applies: the patronymic evidence cannot be set aside on the grounds that the preferred evidence is better corroborated (there is no corroboration), that the error is explained (no mechanism is identified), or that the informant was less proximate (a household member reporting the father's name is highly proximate).

No GPS defensible rationale — better corroboration, explainable error, or less proximate informant — can be invoked without further evidence. (4) Why the convergence nonetheless matters: traditional Norwegian naming (often honouring grandfathers) could produce multiple boys named Anders in the same district and birth year; alternatively, if the project premise 'son of Hans Olsen' rests on a derivative or unverified source, the premise itself may carry the error.
